title_original: “It’s Cringy For Me to See Myself”: Sofia Coppola on Making Marie Antoinette

blocks.text: In April 2024, Sofia Coppola lost her mother, Eleanor. The “cool” (as Sofia describes her), anchoral matriarch of the Coppola family was as proud a mother as she was a wife, her husband Francis and daughter Sofia having mounted two of the most impressive (and unalike) filmographies in the history of cinema, leaving an indelible mark on the medium (her son Roman’s career nothing to balk at either). Likewise, Sofia and the Coppolas were equally proud of Eleanor’s work, which covers a vast range of chronicling expressions. Part video diarist, part multimedia artist, part memoirist, part film director, and more, Eleanor was always chipping away at her own legacy, her own filmography, often in the name of capturing her loved ones at work.

Like her family, she was artistically uncompromising as a filmmaker/documentarian, and Making Marie Antoinette —her final, posthumous film—shows us exactly how. We witness the quintessential Eleanor Coppola approach in the unfettered access to and unapologetic documentation of everything up close and personal. If the film set is a machine, she’s the lone free-floating, nomadic cog, not belonging anywhere but finding a sense of belonging everywhere. But there’s another element to her last movie that gives it a sentimental, inside-baseball perspective.

In 2020, with the pandemic freshly upon us, mother and daughter began shaping the 80+ hours of footage Eleanor had shot on the set of Sofia’s Marie Antoinette in 2005. When Eleanor passed in 2024, Sofia took up the torch to see her mother’s final film to the finish line. As a result, Making Marie Antoinette hones in on her mother’s contagious presence and inner life on set much more than Eleanor’s past behind-the-scenes projects had, combining the voiceover of her mother in daily diary entries in concert with the footage Eleanor shot that day. Instead of merely capturing the machine at work, Making Marie Antoinette offers a more self-reflective, contemplative, and adoring look at Eleanor through the lens of her daughter.

On the heels of the film’s release, we sat down to talk to her about filmmaking as a family affair, her mother’s presence on set, the strange experience of watching herself onscreen, and how her career has evolved in the last twenty years.
The Film Stage: How much of the edit had your mom finished when you took over, and how did you approach directing the edit with her in mind?

Sofia Coppola: She had just been reviewing the footage, but we hadn’t started editing. That was something we were going to do together. She had a friend that was an editor that she wanted to start working on it. But we didn’t actually start the edit, we were just kind of in the review process. So I was going through it with her, and she was explaining what parts she was drawn to. And then I found the editor after she passed and tried to figure out how to finish it in the way she would want it, how we were talking about it.
How long had you been talking about it? I know in the film it says that you both started working on it in 2020, but how active was the conversation about the film between 2020 and 2024?

At that time we were just reviewing the footage and the idea of: could it be a film, which is what she was asking. Because it was never intended to be a film. And I didn’t realize she had so much footage, and that’s when we started looking through it. And then it took a while to actually figure out the team and how we were going to do it. Then this past year, we’ve been editing it, and I met Aaron Matthews, the editor, through a friend of my mom’s, and I’d never worked with him, so it was a whole new process for me.
What is your experience like watching the film? Is it fever-dream-esque? Nostalgic? Stressful?

Yeah, it’s really weird to go back to that time. I mean, I love seeing Jason [Schwartzman] and Kirsten [Dunst] and being on that set without the stress of being in the moment of it. Like, to have some distance. But I do get a little stressed watching it. Like, that feeling of those days on set, how intense it was. And it’s cringy for me to see myself.
In what sense? What makes you cringe?

Just to see myself on camera being a young director, not quite as comfortable being assertive about things. And, like, when I’m irritable. I’m vulnerable in a way that I would never be with a normal behind-the-scenes crew. And I hope there’s always something valuable about a personal look at someone creative. But, as far as being the subject of it, that part’s hard. But I really relied on the editor to be like, “Okay, what do we keep in here?”
When you watch yourself on set, are there specific things that you wish you could go back and do differently?

Now I’m more experienced and I’m more comfortable asking for what I want. I hope for young filmmakers, they see it’s a process and an evolution, that you don’t just show up one day as a fully-formed, experienced person. But there’s things like when we were shooting the big opera scene and we’re changing the extras. And now, as an experienced person, I’m like, “Nobody’s going to notice that the extras weren’t wearing the same costumes in an opera scene thirty minutes later,” you know? [Laughs]. Like, just move them around. We’re all stressing about changing the wigs of the extras. So there are just things that over time you learn. You can get away with a lot.
How did the diaristic element come in, where we’re going through your mom’s diary? Was that something she had put in there or that you added in?

At the end of her life, she wanted her journals, this last book, published. It was third in her book series. So that was something we were also working on at the same time. And the editor helped find the passages that connected to the set. We weren’t originally sure how we were going to put this together. And then luckily, those passages connected with the footage, and so we found that we could make a narration out of it and tie it together.

I know that your parents have been on your sets regularly from the beginning and that you grew up on your dad’s sets, but at the same time, they’re still your parents. Was it ever strange to just have your mom walking around on set with a camera sort of up in your grill?

I’m kind of used to it. So yeah, sometimes. Like when Kirsten and I are trying to gossip and I have my microphone on and I don’t want my mom hearing that conversation. But for the most part, I grew up on set and with her shooting, so I kind of just go with that part of the atmosphere on set. And it was nice to have my mom there, because she was so into it. She’s so encouraging and loved seeing what was all being put together, so it was fun to share that with an enthusiastic mom present.
Did you ever tell her certain things you wanted her to shoot or was she always going off her own directive?

I was just so busy trying to get our days done, and I knew that she had such a great eye that zeros in on interesting details, so I was just happy for her to shoot whatever she thought was interesting. I respect her as a documentarian, and I knew that she loved Milena [Canonero] and the costumes, so I knew that was something she was really into. And then seeing the footage, I saw a lot of things that I had never seen, because I was on the main set. I didn’t realize there were miles of wigs for the extras. I hadn’t even been in that area. So it’s fun to discover.

Marie Antoinette is the biggest shoot of your career to date. What are your reflections on that as you’re watching it? Is that size and budget something you would ever want to do again or are you, like, one and done?

I think at the end I was so fed up I said I’d never do it again, and I don’t feel the same way now, but I definitely learned that I like working in a more hands-on, intimate way. I just think I had that kind of youthful naivete. You take on something without realizing what it really is. I don’t think I’d be as bold now, maybe, but who knows? That’s part of being a creative person—you’re always trying to push things and do things you haven’t done before.
Was it an emotional experience taking up this project? And how did you decide to do that?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, I just felt like my mom wanted it done, so I felt like I was on a mission, like I had to complete this for her. And, in a way, it was a gift that she gave this to me, this footage of this time in my life that I got to revisit and see through her point of view and take the time to complete something for her and spend this time in her work and her point of view. So yeah, it was a big undertaking and emotional.

I didn’t realize how long it would take, and it really took me the [last] year. I didn’t realize how much I had to get into this mode and couldn’t really focus on my other work—to really just take this time. But I’m glad that I did. I’m happy that it’s completed and coming out in the world, because she really wanted it to be done. And the anniversary of Marie Antoinette was our deadline, because it took a while, so we were like, “We have to finish it!” It gave us something to work towards. Otherwise, I don’t know when it would’ve gotten done.
This is also your second documentary in a row after not having worked in documentaries. Is that something you’re interested in continuing more?

It was interesting to just do something different, but now I really miss making a narrative. Getting to imagine a world and create it, because it’s so fun to work with my team and make a world. So I’m looking forward to getting back to my usual thing.
Do you have projects that are currently in production?
No. Now with this finished, I’ll get back to thinking about what’s next. But I’m not sure.
While you were working on Making Marie Antoinette , was your dad ever part of the process? Even if it was just talking about your mom and how she might want something to be edited or put?

Not really, but I showed him. I always show him a rough cut, because he’s so smart about editing and has an opinion, and I value that. But he wasn’t so directly involved. I showed him some cuts. I [actually] showed a lot of cuts to a friend of my mom’s just to be reminded of her perspective and how she would want it. So that helped.
Making Marie Antoinette is now in theaters and arrives on MUBI on November 6. The new 4K restoration of Marie Antoinette is now on MUBI.
